strengths: Technically sound methodology combining MLE with Riemannian optimization and geometry-aware regularization, properly handling noise in different geometric settings
Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets with thorough ablation studies varying noise levels and curvature, showing consistent (if modest) improvements
Excellent reproducibility: detailed pseudocode, hyperparameter specifications, hardware documentation, and code availability indicators
Effective visualizations (Figures 2-3, 5) that clearly demonstrate the method's ability to preserve geometric structure
Honest and explicit discussion of limitations including scalability constraints and acknowledgment of modest empirical gains
Well-motivated problem addressing real applications requiring non-Euclidean representations (cell cycles, phylogenetic trees, DNA analysis)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: using MLE with Riemannian optimization is straightforward application of standard techniques; main contribution (geometry-aware regularization) is relatively incremental
Modest empirical improvements: performance gains over ΔVAE often range 3-10% and sometimes fall within error bars (Table 1: Euclidean ℝ³ shows 0.55±0.04 vs 0.57±0.03)
Narrow experimental scope: all datasets are synthetic or pre-processed; no evaluation on real high-dimensional manifold benchmarks or standard graph datasets; only VAE-variant baselines

Unaddressed scalability limitations: paper acknowledges per-sample parametrization is prohibitive for large datasets but provides no solutions or large-scale experiments; no systematic runtime comparisons
Lack of theoretical analysis: no formal justification for when/why geometry-aware regularization improves learning, no convergence guarantees, no failure mode analysis
Test-time RGD latents strategy appears to be an optimization workaround without clear scalability or practical implementation details

strengths: Well-motivated encoder-less framework that elegantly sidesteps intractable manifold density estimation via Riemannian optimization and geometry-aware regularization
Solid mathematical derivation of the noise-based regularizer (Eqs. 11-16) showing how it implicitly incorporates Riemannian structure weighted by the metric tensor
Comprehensive experimental validation across three biologically distinct datasets (cyclic, hierarchical, evolutionary branching) with multiple manifold geometries
Excellent reproducibility with provided code/data, detailed experimental protocols, explicit hardware specifications, and hyperparameter documentation
Insightful ablation study (Figure 3c) demonstrating the accuracy-geometry tradeoff and providing practical guidance for regularization strength tuning
Generally competitive results showing consistent improvements over S-VAE and ∆VAE baselines in correlation and reconstruction metrics
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily combines existing components (DGD framework, Riemannian optimization, smoothness regularization) without substantial innovation in individual parts

Modest empirical improvements lacking statistical rigor—no p-values, significance tests, or confidence intervals despite having multiple random initializations; many improvements are ≤0.10 in magnitude
Outdated baseline comparisons—only includes S-VAE (2018) and ∆VAE (2019), missing recent hyperbolic and geometry-aware representation learning methods from 2020-2025
Critical hyperparameter tuning opacity—appendix states parameters were 'tuned for each model and dataset' without specifying validation procedures, risking bias toward the proposed method
Theoretical gaps in regularizer derivation—Taylor expansion ignores O(‖ε‖⁴) terms without discussing failure regimes; trace approximation of Hessian (Eq. 16) may lose important geometric structure

Questionable evidence of meaningful geometry learning—Table 1 shows nearly identical performance across fundamentally different manifolds (Euclidean, Sphere, Torus) for cell cycle data, raising whether geometric constraints are actually learned or method is robust to incorrect manifold choice

Weak generative quality and downstream utility—RGD discrimination scores (0.38-0.63) suggest poor distribution learning; downstream classification accuracy modest (0.31-0.90) using only simple linear models
Scalability limitations—experiments limited to ≤50D; Table 4 shows methods 'break' computationally; no analysis of memory scaling or applicability to high-dimensional problems

Incomplete experimental methodology—no initialization/seed sensitivity analysis, unfair UMAP comparison (dimensionality reduction vs. generative model), visualization quality issues, and limited exploration of failure modes

Unclear method applicability and presentation—weak justification that encoder-less approach avoids density estimation (regularizer acts as latent density prior); three case studies don't provide unified insights about when practitioners should use this method
